thread.title: Intraday Update: Can Anything Rattle the Dow Industrials? - Barron's

title: Intraday Update: Can Anything Rattle the Dow Industrials? - Barron's
text:
Brett Arends Updated May 16, 2018 1:28 p.m. ET
Money got more expensive again Wednesday morning. Ten-year Treasury yields broke above 3.09%, their highest levels since the summer of 2011, before easing back to 3.08%. Interest rates on three-month Treasury bills firmed above 1.93%, their highest levels since before Lehman Bros. collapsed, before also easing back to 1.925%. Illustration: Bloomberg News
Awkward fact: When rates were last this level, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was deemed to be worth no more than 11,000 to 12,500. Currently it’s about 24,700. It was broadly flat Wednesday morning, along with the broader Standard & Poor’s 500 index. Small-caps were higher, with the Russell 2000 index rising about 0.5%.
The Wall Street sales machine has spent most of the past decade explaining why lower interest rates were great for stocks. Expect them to spend the coming months, and possibly years, explaining why higher rates great for stocks too . Sure, why not?
The kumbaya chorus isn’t just on Wall Street. South Korea’s Kospi index edged into the black despite a new bout of saber-rattling by its northern neighbor. North Korea is threatening to pull out of the forthcoming planned meeting between Kim Jong-un and Donald Trump over demands it commit to abandoning its nuclear program.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 eased just 0.4% despite news the economy actually shrank last quarter, and grew much less than previously thought in the previous three months.
If recession and the threat of nuclear war aren't enough to rattle investors, why should expensive money?
Tesla (TSLA) was broadly flat following news that George Soros has bought $35 million of the company’s bonds. The liberal billionaire, subject of a thousand right-wing conspiracy theories, also loaded up on Netflix (NFLX) and Amazon.com (AMZN). Netflix and Amazon were both up nearly 1%.
It's probably enough to freak out armies of self-described “conservatives." They're already having conniptions that newly resurgent Twitter (TWTR), up around 0.5%, is trying to restrict the incendiary speech it publishes—almost like it’s a private company or something.
Apple (AAPL) rose 0.8% despite a report that “investors” recently cut their holdings by the "most since at least 2008." According to a detailed review of filings, institutional investors in the first quarter sold 153 million Apple shares. By our back-of-the-envelope calculations, it would seem that this means other investors—plus the company itself—bought 153 million shares during the same period. But what do we know?
S&P 500 : +0.6% to 2726.52 Dow 30 : +85.15 points, or 0.3%, to 24,791.56 Nasdaq : +0.8% to 7409.52
